### Question 1

Imagine you want to know if extra sunlight makes a plant grow taller. You are the one who decides how much sunlight each plant gets, so sunlight is the thing you change on purpose. That 'thing you change on purpose' has a name in research: the independent variable. It is called independent because nothing else in the study sets it; you set it, and then you watch what happens to everything else.

### Question 2

Saying 'make the room warm' is vague, but saying 'set the thermostat to 22 degrees Celsius' tells anyone exactly what to do. Research works the same way. The word 'anxiety' is fuzzy, so investigators write down the exact steps: 'a score from 0 to 10 on this checklist, collected before class.' Those steps are the operational definition, and they let a totally different school run the same study and get numbers that can honestly be compared.

### Question 3

Some answers are labels and some answers are amounts. 'My blood type is AB' is a label, like a team color; AB is not 'more' than A, it is just a different bucket. 'I slept 7.5 hours' is an amount, and you can land anywhere along the ruler, even halfway between two marks. Labels with no ruler behind them are categorical or nominal variables, and spotting which kind you have tells you what you can and cannot do with the data.

### Question 4

A dimmer switch has settings: off, low, and bright. Those are three settings of one switch, not three different switches on the wall. In a study, the thing you turn up or down is the variable, and each setting you actually use is called a level. So 'no music, soft music, loud music' is one variable with three levels, and almost any design can be summarized that way: which variable, and how many levels of it.

### Question 5

Say you try a new study app and your quiz score climbs 8 points. That sounds convincing until you remember scores often climb anyway as you get used to the course and the quiz format. So the researcher also follows a similar group of students who study the usual way. That group is the comparison, or control, group, and it shows how much scores would have moved without the app, so the app only gets credit for the difference between the two.

### Question 6

A cross-sectional study is a class photo: everyone in one picture on one day, so you can compare people to each other. A longitudinal study is the pencil marks on a doorframe: the same person, measured again and again over years, so you can watch that individual change. Snapshot versus growth chart is the whole difference, and it decides whether the study can honestly say anything about change over time.

### Question 7

Suppose you want to know which of two backpacks feels lighter. Handing one to you and the other to your taller friend is a messy test, because you two are simply built differently. Carrying both yourself, one after the other, is a fair test, because everything about the carrier stays the same. That is a within-subjects design. The catch is that you are tired by the second backpack, so researchers switch up the order between people to keep that from fooling them.

### Question 8

Picture fence posts along a 12-meter path with one post every 3 meters. You get posts at 3, 6, 9, and 12 meters, which is four, but you also need one at the very start of the path. That starting post is the baseline measurement. Intervals plus one starting point is the rule, and forgetting the starting post is exactly how people undercount the time points in a follow-up study.

### Question 9

Deal 96 index cards into 4 stacks, one card at a time, until the deck runs out, and every stack ends up with 24. Study conditions get filled the same way. Researchers aim for equal stacks on purpose, because a comparison in which one condition has 60 people and another has 12 gives you shaky information about the small group, no matter how many people are in the study overall.

### Question 10

You are testing whether a new bike chain makes you faster, but on some rides the wind is at your back. The wind is not the chain and it is not your speed, yet it clearly moves your speed around. In a study, that uninvited extra influence is an extraneous variable. Careful planners either shut it out, by only riding on calm days, or at minimum write down how windy each ride was so it can be sorted out afterward.

### Question 11

Imagine two people arguing about whether a room is 'too loud.' One says it feels noisy, the other says it is fine, and nothing gets settled until someone says 'we will hold a sound meter in the doorway at 8 a.m. and read the number.' That sentence names the tool, the place, and the time, so two strangers land on the same answer. Saying what hydration means, or why it matters, does not tell the person with the clipboard what to actually do; naming the instrument and the moment does.

### Question 12

Think of a shop with 2 cone types and 3 flavors. Every cone can hold every flavor, so you sketch a grid of 2 rows by 3 columns and count 6 possible orders, not 5. A crossed study design is literally that grid: each square is a real group of participants receiving one specific combination, which is why you multiply the numbers of levels instead of adding them.
